paragraphs.source_en: In the third month of Tenshō 8, at the height of spring, the beacon fires of war flared once more, and the old enemies—the Takeda and Tokugawa clans—again embarked upon a great conflict.

paragraphs.source_en: Both Ieyasu and Katsuyori racked their brains in an effort to retain the strategic advantage. paragraphs.source_en: For Ieyasu, Takatenjin Castle in Katsuyori's hands, together with the fortifications at Koyama Castle, Sagara, and elsewhere, held the key to strategy in Tōtōmi. These strongholds had once been held by Ieyasu, but on the seventeenth day of the sixth month of Tenshō 2, Katsuyori had seized them back, making them the foundations of his power in the region. For the six years since then, Ieyasu had watched covetously, waiting for an opportunity to take them back.

paragraphs.source_en: Naturally, Takatenjin Castle also held extraordinary significance for Katsuyori. The castle that even his father had failed to conquer had fallen to Katsuyori, becoming his proudest achievement for inspiring his troops and displaying his might to Nobunaga and Ieyasu. If Ieyasu took Takatenjin Castle, not only would all Tōtōmi fall within his grasp, but Suruga itself would immediately come under threat.
